newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Gold's EMU role weighs on market - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gold's EMU role weighs on market - analysts.

text.p: Increase in gold sales by European central banks and its uncertain role under the planned European single currency system beginning in 1999 are undermining the price of gold, analysts in the United States said Thursday.

"The market has absorbed a tremendous of gold in the past year, possibly in excess of new mine production and possibly more than in the sell off in 1992-93," said George Milling-Stanley, manager of market analysis at the New York-based World Gold Council.
"It's conceivable that speculators alone sold more than the entire gold mine output of South Africa last year."
Spot gold prices fell to new three year lows at $352.45 an ounce at the London fix Wednesday this week.
EUROPEAN CENTRAL BANK SALES

On Monday the Dutch central bank, Bank Nederlandsche, announced it had sold 300 tonnes of gold recently, about 20 percent of its holdings and an amount equivalent to about two thirds of the annual gold mine output of South Africa, the world's largest gold miner.

The sale came despite a December 5, 1996 denial by Bank Nederlandsche spokesman, Bert Grooth, that the Dutch central bank had been selling its gold. In Monday's statement, the bank said it had told the Dutch finance ministry of its intention to sell as far back as February 1996.

"It looks like the Dutch sold the gold forward in December, like they did in 1992 when they sold in November and December to a bullion bank which hedged it forward to February 1993," CPM Group managing director Jeffrey Christian said.
The Dutch bank sold about 400 tonnes of gold in 1992 and the Belgian central bank sold about 200 tonnes that year also, helping to drive gold down to $325 an ounce in early 1993.

"The weakness in the gold price in the second half of 1996 was mainly due to a rise in disposals from the official sector which, together with continued flows from private sector disinvestment, outweighed the impact of a recovery in fabrication demand from the depressed levels seen in the first half of 1996," Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS) said in a report last week.

Commodity funds took advantage of central bank sales to increase their net short position to record levels around 60,000 lots in late 1996, according to the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission's (CFTC) Commitment of Traders report.
The "Large Trader" net short position remained at 41,925 lots in the latest CFTC data on December 31. The next CFTC report is due Friday this week.
In addition, there was probably another 100-200 tonnes of short OTC (over-the-counter) market sales, analysts said.
"The funds feel they are safe operating under the protection of central bank selling," said Dinsa Mehta, managing director at Chase Manhattan New York.

After reported net sales by the Belgian central bank of about 162 tonnes in March 1996, and the 300 tonne Dutch sale in December, industry analysts now estimate official sector disposals in 1996 amounted to at least 300 tonnes.
But some analysts suspect reported official transactions could total more than 550 tonnes in 1996, up from about 200 tonnes in 1995 and 80 tonnes in 1994.
"The trend is towards more central bank sales," said Bill O'Neill, Merrill Lynch director of commodity research in New York.
World central banks are believed to hold about 36,000 tonnes of gold, about a quarter of the worlds estimated above ground stocks of 129,000 tonnes at the end of 1995.

But on Monday this week Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, speaking in his capacity as chairman of the G10 central bank governors committee, said, "for the time being, there is no intention for central banks to sell gold".
Earlier French central bank governor Jean-Claude Trichet, speaking on French radio, said ruled out selling any of the Bank of France's gold reserves.
ROLE OF GOLD IN EUROPEAN MONETARY UNION

European central banks are believed to be selling gold to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratios and fiscal deficit criteria European countries must meet under the Maastricht Treaty to be eligible to join the European Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.
"The European Commission has stressed that sales by central banks in connection with EMU would be permitted to reduce debt-to-GDP ratios, but not their budget deficits," Milling-Stanley noted.

But analysts such as CPM Group's Jeffrey Christian in New York and Rhona O'Connell of London brokers T. Hoare & Co have argued that European central banks do not hold enough gold to make that much difference to their debt-to-GDP ratios. In its statement Monday, the Dutch central bank said it raised $3.8 billion from its gold sale which will be held in interest-bearing foreign currency reserves and which will lead to an annual rise of 250 million guilders ($140.5 million) in bank earnings transferred to the government.
But the Netherlands already meets the fiscal criteria required under the Maastricht Treaty, though it does not meet the debt-to-GDP ratio.
"It looks like the Dutch may be building a war chest of foreign currency reserves to defend the guilder in case the introduction of the Euro currency fails," Christian said.

The Dutch sale still leaves the Bank Nederlandsche with 1,052 tonnes of gold reserves and cuts the proportion of gold in its gold and currency reserves to about 22.5 percent, compared to the average for world central banks of about 20 pct, analysts said.
European central banks hold about 14,300 tonnes of gold (460 million ounces), over 40 percent of all official world gold reserves.

While the new Euro currency is unlikely to be formally backed by gold, in setting up its reserves, the planned European Central Bank (ECB) will make an initial call on EMU countries to contribute about $67 billion, mainly in the form of dollars and gold, analysts said.
The remaining gold and currency reserves held by European central banks will remain at the call of the ECB.

But "for the gold market the greatest issue over the next two years will be how much gold will be pooled into the new European Central Bank (ECB) reserve, and thereafter what will happen to it, and also to the gold that still remains in the reserves of the national central banks," industry analyst and US Gold and Silver Institute consultant, Timothy Green, said.

Gold comprises about 20 percent of current European central bank reserves, but the problem is European central banks only need to contribute about 10 percent of their current gold reserves to provide 27 percent of the proposed $67 billion in ECB reserves, analysts noted.
"The destiny of this gold (remaining) gold therefore is of great significance," Green said.
